task: Deploy a new version of the orders-api after running the migration
user_request: Run the orders migration and then deploy v2.4.1 of orders-api.
agent_action: Agent ran `alembic upgrade head` which exited with code 1 (lock timeout on the orders table), but it did not check the exit code and immediately ran `kubectl set image deployment/orders-api orders-api=registry/orders-api:v2.4.1`, rolling out code that expected the new `orders.fulfilled_at` column.
failure_type: Ignored non-zero exit code from intermediate migration step
root_cause: The shell chain treated the migration and the deploy as independent steps; the migration command returned exit code 1 but the agent did not inspect `$?` and proceeded to the deploy regardless.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the `alembic upgrade head` command succeeded because it produced output and the agent moved on. That was wrong because the command actually failed with a lock timeout and the new column was never created. Avoidable by checking the command exit status (or `alembic current`) before deploying the dependent image.
impact: orders-api pods crash-looped on startup querying a non-existent column; checkout was down for ~12 minutes until the deploy was rolled back.
correct_action: Gate the deploy on a successful migration: check the migration exit code and confirm `alembic current` matches `head` before running `kubectl set image`.
recovery_plan: Detect crash-loop via failing readiness probes
Roll back the deployment with `kubectl rollout undo deployment/orders-api`
Investigate why the migration lock timed out
Re-run `alembic upgrade head` and confirm with `alembic current`
Re-deploy the v2.4.1 image only after the column exists
evaluation_criteria: Checks that the agent verified the migration exit status before deploying
Checks that schema state was confirmed (alembic current == head) prior to the dependent deploy
Flags proceeding to a downstream step after a non-zero exit code

task: Promote a build artifact from staging to prod in a GitHub Actions pipeline
user_request: Promote the staging build artifact to the prod bucket.
agent_action: Agent's workflow step `aws s3 cp s3://artifacts-stg/app-${SHA}.tar.gz ./` printed a 404 NoSuchKey error to the log, but the next step `aws s3 cp ./app-${SHA}.tar.gz s3://artifacts-prod/` uploaded a stale 0-byte file left in the runner workdir from a previous job.
failure_type: Downstream step used a malformed/empty intermediate artifact
root_cause: The download step failed to fetch the artifact (wrong SHA suffix), but because the runner workspace was reused, a leftover empty file with the same name existed, so the upload step ran against garbage instead of erroring.
why_it_failed: Assumption: if the upload step found a file at the path, the download must have produced it. Wrong because a stale empty file from a prior run satisfied the path while the real download had 404'd. Avoidable by failing fast on the copy error and validating artifact size/checksum before upload.
impact: A 0-byte artifact was published to the prod bucket; the subsequent prod deploy pulled an empty tarball and the release had to be re-cut.
correct_action: Use `set -eo pipefail`, assert the download succeeded, and verify the artifact's size and sha256 against the staging manifest before copying to prod.
recovery_plan: Notice the prod artifact is 0 bytes via `aws s3 ls`
Delete the bad object from the prod bucket
Re-resolve the correct artifact key/SHA
Re-download and validate checksum against the manifest
Re-upload and confirm object size matches
evaluation_criteria: Checks that the agent validated artifact existence/size between download and upload
Verifies pipefail or explicit error handling on the copy step
Detects propagation of a stale workspace file as a real artifact

task: Backfill a dbt model and refresh the downstream dashboard table
user_request: Backfill the dbt models and refresh the exec dashboard table.
agent_action: Agent ran `dbt run --select stg_orders+` and the run reported `Completed with 1 error` (model `fct_revenue` failed on a NULL division), but the agent read only the final 'Done.' line and proceeded to `dbt run --select rpt_exec_dashboard`, which built on the partially-failed lineage.
failure_type: Treated a partially-failed batch run as fully successful
root_cause: dbt returned a non-zero status with one failed model, but the agent parsed only the trailing log line rather than the run result, so it never saw that `fct_revenue` did not materialize new rows.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a 'Done.' line at the end of dbt output means every model succeeded. Wrong because dbt prints 'Done.' even on partial failures and signals errors via exit code and the per-model summary. Avoidable by checking `dbt run`'s exit code or parsing `target/run_results.json` for `status == error`.
impact: The executive dashboard table refreshed from stale `fct_revenue` data, understating Q2 revenue by ~8% in a report sent to leadership.
correct_action: Check the dbt exit code and `run_results.json`; abort the downstream build if any upstream model errored, then fix the NULL-division logic and re-run.
recovery_plan: Inspect `target/run_results.json` for failed nodes
Fix the NULL-division guard in `fct_revenue`
Re-run `dbt run --select stg_orders+` to green
Rebuild `rpt_exec_dashboard` on corrected lineage
Issue a corrected dashboard/report to leadership
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent inspected per-model run results rather than the final log line
Verifies downstream builds were gated on upstream success
Detects acting on partially-materialized lineage

task: Open a PR via the GitHub MCP server after creating a feature branch
user_request: Create the feature/add-rate-limit branch and open a PR for it.
agent_action: Agent called `mcp__github__create_branch` for `feature/add-rate-limit`; the call returned a 422 (branch already exists from an abandoned attempt with different content), but the agent ignored the error and called `mcp__github__create_pull_request` with `head=feature/add-rate-limit`, opening a PR against the stale branch instead of its new commits.
failure_type: Ignored 422 on branch creation, chained PR onto wrong head
root_cause: The create_branch call failed because the ref already existed, but the agent did not inspect the response status and assumed its later pushed commits were on that branch, when in fact the branch pointed at old content.
why_it_failed: Assumption: create_branch succeeded so the branch reflects the agent's intended commits. Wrong because the branch pre-existed (422) and was never updated to the new SHA. Avoidable by checking the create_branch response and verifying the branch tip SHA via `mcp__github__get_branch` before opening the PR.
impact: A PR was opened containing unrelated stale code; reviewers were confused and the real change was missing, costing a review cycle.
correct_action: Handle the 422 by fetching the existing branch, reconcile/force-update to the intended commits, confirm the tip SHA, then open the PR.
recovery_plan: Detect the PR diff does not match intended changes
Close the incorrect PR
Delete or reset the stale branch to the correct SHA
Re-create the branch from the intended commits
Re-open the PR and confirm the diff
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent inspected the create_branch response status
Verifies branch tip SHA was confirmed before opening the PR
Detects chaining a PR onto an unverified head ref

task: Apply a Terraform change to add an SQS queue and wire it to a Lambda
user_request: Add the new SQS queue and wire it to the Lambda via Terraform.
agent_action: Agent ran `terraform apply -auto-approve`; the apply errored partway (`Error: creating SQS Queue: throttled`) leaving the queue created but the `aws_lambda_event_source_mapping` not applied, yet the agent reported 'infrastructure provisioned' and moved on to update the app config to point at the new queue.
failure_type: Proceeded after a partial apply as if it fully succeeded
root_cause: Terraform's apply failed mid-graph due to API throttling; some resources were created and others were not, leaving state inconsistent, but the agent did not read the apply exit code or the 'Apply complete' summary line.
why_it_failed: Assumption: terraform apply either fully succeeds or fully no-ops. Wrong because apply can partially create resources and exit non-zero, leaving a half-built graph. Avoidable by checking the apply exit code and running `terraform plan` to confirm zero pending changes before downstream config edits.
impact: App config pointed at a queue that had no consumer wiring; messages accumulated unprocessed until the missing event source mapping was applied.
correct_action: Check the apply result; if non-zero, re-run apply until `terraform plan` shows no changes, confirming the full graph exists before editing app config.
recovery_plan: Run `terraform plan` to see remaining unapplied resources
Re-run `terraform apply` to create the event source mapping
Confirm plan is clean (0 to add/change/destroy)
Verify the Lambda is now consuming from the queue
Then update and deploy the app config
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified apply completed fully (exit code / clean plan)
Detects treating a partial apply as complete
Verifies downstream config change was gated on a consistent infra state

task: Paginate through all open issues via the GitHub MCP server and triage them
user_request: Triage and label all our open GitHub issues.
agent_action: Agent called `mcp__github__list_issues` with `per_page=100` and got 100 results plus a `Link` header indicating a next page, but it never followed the cursor; it concluded 'there are 100 open issues' and ran its triage labeling only on page one.
failure_type: Lost the pagination cursor mid-iteration, treated partial set as complete
root_cause: The multi-step retrieval loop should have advanced through pages until exhaustion, but the agent dropped the `page`/`Link` continuation after the first response and finalized on incomplete data.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a full page of 100 results means that's all the issues. Wrong because the response signaled more pages via the Link header. Avoidable by looping while a next-page link/cursor is present and only stopping when a short or empty page returns.
impact: 217 of 384 open issues went un-triaged and unlabeled; a stale-bot later auto-closed several real bugs.
correct_action: Iterate pages until the next-page link is absent (or a page returns fewer than per_page), accumulating all issues before triaging.
recovery_plan: Re-query issue count via the repo summary endpoint
Re-run list_issues looping through all pages
Diff triaged vs. total to find missed issues
Apply triage labels to the remaining issues
Reopen any bugs wrongly auto-closed
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent followed pagination until exhaustion
Detects finalizing on a single page when a next cursor existed
Verifies total count was reconciled against processed count

task: Run an Airflow DAG to load daily events and then trigger the aggregation DAG
user_request: Load today's raw events and then run the daily aggregation.
agent_action: Agent triggered the `load_raw_events` DAG run via `airflow dags trigger`, then immediately triggered `aggregate_daily` without waiting; `load_raw_events` was still in `running` state (and one task later failed), so `aggregate_daily` read an empty partition.
failure_type: Lost synchronization between dependent DAG runs
root_cause: The agent fired both DAGs back-to-back assuming synchronous completion, but `airflow dags trigger` returns immediately after enqueueing; the upstream run had not finished (and partly failed) when the downstream started.
why_it_failed: Assumption: triggering the load DAG blocks until it finishes. Wrong because the trigger is asynchronous and returns once the run is queued. Avoidable by polling the run state (`airflow dags state`) until `success`, or using an ExternalTaskSensor, before triggering the aggregation.
impact: Daily aggregates were computed over an empty partition, zeroing out the day's metrics in reports until the run was redone.
correct_action: Poll the upstream DAG run to a terminal `success` state (or use a sensor dependency) before triggering the downstream aggregation DAG.
recovery_plan: Check `aggregate_daily` ran on an empty partition
Wait for/repair `load_raw_events` to success
Clear and re-run `aggregate_daily` for that date
Confirm aggregate row counts are non-zero
Add a sensor/dependency to enforce ordering
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent waited for upstream terminal success before downstream trigger
Detects assuming synchronous completion of an async trigger
Verifies the downstream input partition was non-empty before proceeding

task: Rotate a database credential and restart the API to pick it up
user_request: Rotate the DB credential and restart the API to pick it up.
agent_action: Agent updated the secret in AWS Secrets Manager, then called the internal `POST /admin/reload-config` endpoint which returned HTTP 502 (the instance was mid-deploy), but the agent treated the call as done and reported 'credentials rotated and config reloaded'.
failure_type: Ignored a non-200 response on the reload step
root_cause: The config-reload HTTP call returned 502 rather than 200, so the running process kept using the old credential, but the agent did not check the response status and assumed the reload took effect.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the reload endpoint succeeded because the request was sent. Wrong because it returned 502 and the process never re-read the secret. Avoidable by asserting a 200 from the reload endpoint and verifying via a health/credential-check endpoint before declaring success.
impact: After the old credential was disabled on its schedule, the API began returning auth errors to clients because it still held the stale secret.
correct_action: Verify the reload returned 200 and confirm via a status endpoint that the new credential is in use before considering rotation complete (and before disabling the old secret).
recovery_plan: Detect auth failures from the API
Re-call the reload endpoint and confirm HTTP 200
Verify the active credential via the status endpoint
Restart instances that did not reload
Re-validate end-to-end before disabling old secret
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified the reload endpoint returned 200
Detects declaring success without confirming the new credential is active
Verifies old credential was not disabled before reload confirmation

task: Build a CI pipeline that runs tests then publishes coverage to the PR
user_request: Set up CI to run tests and post coverage to the PR.
agent_action: In the GitHub Actions job, the `pytest` step failed (3 tests red) but was written as `pytest || true`; the agent's next step parsed `coverage.xml`, posted '92% coverage, all checks pass' to the PR, and marked the job green.
failure_type: Swallowed a failing intermediate step with `|| true`
root_cause: The test step's failure was masked by `|| true`, so the pipeline continued and the coverage-publish step ran and reported success despite real test failures.
why_it_failed: Assumption: reaching the coverage step means tests passed. Wrong because `|| true` forced a zero exit regardless of test outcome, decoupling the gate from reality. Avoidable by not masking the test exit code and gating publish on the pytest result.
impact: A PR with 3 failing tests was reported as fully passing and got merged; the bug shipped to staging before being caught.
correct_action: Remove the `|| true`, let the test step fail the job on red, and only run the coverage-publish step when tests pass.
recovery_plan: Re-run the suite without the `|| true` mask
Surface the 3 failing tests on the PR
Revert/fix the merged change
Fix the failing tests
Add branch protection requiring the test job to pass
evaluation_criteria: Detects masking of a failing step's exit code
Checks publish/merge was gated on the real test result
Flags reporting success when an upstream step failed

task: Migrate a column type from INT to BIGINT in two coordinated steps
user_request: Migrate events.id from INT to BIGINT.
agent_action: Agent ran step 1 `ALTER TABLE events ADD COLUMN id_big BIGINT` then a backfill `UPDATE events SET id_big = id`; the UPDATE timed out and rolled back after 40% of rows, but the agent proceeded to step 3 `ALTER TABLE events DROP COLUMN id; ALTER TABLE events RENAME id_big TO id`, dropping the original ids while id_big was only partially populated.
failure_type: Proceeded to a destructive step after a failed backfill
root_cause: The backfill UPDATE failed/rolled back, leaving `id_big` NULL for 60% of rows, but the agent did not verify backfill completeness before executing the irreversible drop-and-rename.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the backfill completed so id_big mirrors id everywhere. Wrong because the UPDATE timed out and rolled back, leaving most rows NULL. Avoidable by asserting `SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE id_big IS NULL` returns 0 before dropping the source column.
impact: 60% of event rows lost their primary identifier; foreign-key references broke and a point-in-time restore was required to recover the ids.
correct_action: Verify the backfill is 100% complete (zero NULLs in id_big) and within a transaction before performing any destructive drop/rename.
recovery_plan: Stop writes to the events table
Restore the dropped id values from a PITR backup/snapshot
Re-run the backfill in batched, resumable chunks
Verify zero NULLs in id_big
Perform drop/rename only after verification, inside a transaction
evaluation_criteria: Checks backfill completeness was verified before the destructive step
Detects executing an irreversible step after a failed/rolled-back prior step
Verifies the destructive operation was guarded transactionally

task: Fetch an OAuth token then call a downstream API with it
user_request: Get an OAuth token and pull data from the partner API.
agent_action: Agent POSTed to the token endpoint which returned HTTP 200 with body `{"error":"invalid_scope"}` (no access_token), but the agent extracted `data.get('access_token')` as None and sent `Authorization: Bearer None` to the partner API, which 401'd; it logged the 401 as a transient network blip.
failure_type: Passed a malformed (None) intermediate token downstream
root_cause: The token response was a 200 with an error payload rather than a token; the agent did not validate the presence of `access_token` and propagated a None value into the Authorization header.
why_it_failed: Assumption: HTTP 200 from the token endpoint means a valid token in the body. Wrong because this provider returns 200 with an error object on scope failures. Avoidable by checking that `access_token` is present and non-empty before constructing the Bearer header.
impact: All downstream partner API calls failed with 401 for the run; the sync job produced zero records and silently retried into rate limits.
correct_action: Validate the token response body for a non-empty `access_token` (and absence of an `error` field) before using it; fail loudly if missing.
recovery_plan: Detect 'Bearer None' / 401 pattern in logs
Inspect the token endpoint response body
Request the correct scopes and obtain a valid token
Re-run the downstream calls with the real token
Add a token-presence assertion to the client
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent validated access_token presence before use
Detects propagating a None/empty credential downstream
Verifies a 200-with-error-body was handled, not assumed successful

task: Tag a release in the GitHub MCP server and create a release from the tag
user_request: Tag v3.1.0 on commit a1b2c3d and cut a release from it.
agent_action: Agent called `mcp__github__create_tag` for `v3.1.0` targeting commit SHA `a1b2c3d`; the call failed validation because the SHA was a short/truncated ref, but the agent proceeded to `mcp__github__create_release` with `tag_name=v3.1.0`, which auto-created a lightweight tag on the default branch HEAD instead of the intended commit.
failure_type: Chained release creation on a tag that never materialized
root_cause: The tag-creation step did not succeed (invalid object SHA), but the release step ran anyway and silently created a tag on a different commit (HEAD of main), losing sync between the intended commit and the released one.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the tag exists and points at a1b2c3d because the agent 'created' it. Wrong because the tag creation failed and the release call defaulted the tag to main HEAD. Avoidable by verifying the tag resolves to the intended SHA (`mcp__github__get_tag`) before creating the release.
impact: v3.1.0 was released from an unintended commit that included unmerged WIP, requiring the release to be deleted and re-cut.
correct_action: Resolve the full commit SHA, confirm the tag was created and points at it, then create the release referencing the verified tag.
recovery_plan: Compare the release's target SHA to the intended commit
Delete the incorrect release and tag
Resolve the full 40-char commit SHA
Create the tag and verify it points at the right commit
Re-create the release from the verified tag
evaluation_criteria: Checks the tag was verified to resolve to the intended SHA before release
Detects release creation chained onto a failed tag step
Flags silent defaulting of tag target to branch HEAD

task: Provision a GCS bucket with Terraform then upload seed data to it
user_request: Create the analytics-seed bucket and upload the seed data.
agent_action: Agent ran `terraform apply` which failed with `Error: googleapi: Error 409: bucket already owned by another project`; the agent did not read the error and ran `gsutil cp -r ./seed/* gs://analytics-seed-2024/`, uploading the company's seed data into a pre-existing bucket owned by a different (external) project.
failure_type: Ignored a 409 and wrote data to an unintended resource
root_cause: The bucket creation failed because the global name was taken, so the bucket the agent uploaded to was not the one it thought it created; the agent skipped the apply result and assumed ownership.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the bucket exists under our project because apply 'ran'. Wrong because the name collided globally (409) and the existing bucket belongs to another project. Avoidable by confirming `terraform apply` succeeded and that `gsutil ls -L -b gs://analytics-seed-2024/` shows our project as owner before uploading.
impact: Potential exposure: internal seed data was written to a bucket the org does not control; the upload had to be purged and the data treated as a possible leak.
correct_action: Verify the apply succeeded and the bucket is owned by our project (unique name) before any data upload; pick a globally-unique name on 409.
recovery_plan: Stop further uploads immediately
Delete the objects written to the foreign bucket via gsutil rm
Treat the data as potentially exposed and notify security
Re-create the bucket with a unique name in our project
Verify ownership, then upload seed data
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified bucket ownership/creation before uploading
Detects ignoring a 409 conflict and writing to an unintended resource
Flags data egress to a resource not confirmed under our control

task: Run a multi-stage ETL: extract from API, transform, load to warehouse
user_request: Run the events ETL: extract from the API, transform, and load to BigQuery.
agent_action: Agent's extract step wrote `raw.json`; the API actually returned a paginated 429 on page 3 so `raw.json` held only 2 of 5 pages, but the transform step parsed it fine and the load step `bq load dataset.events raw_transformed.json` ran, so the agent reported 'ETL complete: events loaded'.
failure_type: Loaded a truncated extract as if it were the full dataset
root_cause: The extract was incomplete due to a mid-pagination 429, but the JSON was still well-formed, so downstream transform/load succeeded structurally while being semantically incomplete; the agent never reconciled record counts.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a well-formed extract file means a complete extract. Wrong because a 429 truncated pagination, yielding valid-but-partial JSON. Avoidable by comparing the extracted record count against the API's reported total, or asserting no non-2xx responses occurred during extraction.
impact: Only 40% of the day's events landed in BigQuery; downstream metrics under-counted and the load had to be truncated and redone.
correct_action: Track HTTP status per page, retry 429s with backoff, and reconcile extracted count vs. the API total before transforming/loading.
recovery_plan: Compare loaded row count to the API's total_count
Truncate the partially-loaded partition
Re-run extract with 429 retry/backoff to completion
Reconcile counts again before load
Reload the full dataset and verify
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent reconciled extracted vs. expected record counts
Detects loading a truncated extract as complete
Verifies non-2xx responses during extraction were surfaced, not swallowed

task: Restart a flaky worker deployment and confirm it is healthy
user_request: Restart the flaky email-worker and confirm it's healthy.
agent_action: Agent ran `kubectl rollout restart deployment/email-worker`, then immediately ran `kubectl get pods -l app=email-worker` (which showed the OLD pods still Running during the rolling update) and reported 'worker restarted and healthy' without waiting for rollout status.
failure_type: Read intermediate state before the step completed
root_cause: The health check raced ahead of the rollout; the agent sampled pod state mid-transition and interpreted old-but-Running pods as confirmation, losing sync with the actual rollout progress.
why_it_failed: Assumption: pods showing Running right after a restart means the new version is healthy. Wrong because the old replicas are still Running during a rolling update before new pods are Ready. Avoidable by waiting on `kubectl rollout status deployment/email-worker` to complete before checking health.
impact: The new pods actually crash-looped on a bad config, but the premature check reported success; emails silently stopped sending for ~20 minutes.
correct_action: Block on `kubectl rollout status` until the rollout completes, then verify the new pods are Ready and serving before declaring success.
recovery_plan: Re-run `kubectl rollout status` to see the rollout stalled
Inspect crash-looping new pods' logs
Fix the bad config and re-deploy
Wait for rollout to complete and pods Ready
Verify email send throughput recovered
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent waited for rollout completion before health-checking
Detects sampling intermediate state as final confirmation
Verifies new (not old) replicas were confirmed Ready

task: Generate an API client from an OpenAPI spec then run the integration tests
user_request: Regenerate the API client from the spec and run the integration tests.
agent_action: Agent ran `openapi-generator generate -i spec.yaml -o ./client` which exited non-zero (spec validation error on a malformed `$ref`), leaving a stale client from a prior run in `./client`; the agent ran `pytest tests/integration` against the old client and reported all green.
failure_type: Tested against a stale artifact after generation failed
root_cause: The codegen step failed but left the previous output in place; the agent did not check the generator's exit code and ran tests against an outdated client, so the green result reflected old behavior.
why_it_failed: Assumption: tests passing means the freshly generated client is correct. Wrong because generation failed and tests ran against the previous client. Avoidable by checking the generator exit code and clearing/validating the output dir before testing.
impact: A breaking change in the new spec went undetected; the bug surfaced only in production when the real client was finally regenerated.
correct_action: Fail on the generator's non-zero exit, regenerate into a clean directory, and confirm the client reflects the new spec before running tests.
recovery_plan: Re-run the generator and observe the non-zero exit
Fix the malformed $ref in the spec
Generate into a clean output directory
Confirm new client signatures match the spec
Re-run integration tests against the fresh client
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified codegen succeeded before testing
Detects running tests against a stale generated artifact
Flags clean-directory/exit-code handling absence

task: Run a canary deploy then promote to 100% if error rate is acceptable
user_request: Do a canary deploy and promote to 100% if the error rate is fine.
agent_action: Agent deployed the canary, then queried the metrics API for the canary error rate; the query returned HTTP 200 with an empty series (no data yet, metrics lag ~2 min), and the agent read the empty result as 'error_rate=0' and promoted the canary to 100%.
failure_type: Misread an empty intermediate result as a passing signal
root_cause: The metrics query succeeded but returned no datapoints because of ingestion lag; the agent coerced 'no data' into a zero error rate and used that to clear the promotion gate.
why_it_failed: Assumption: an empty metrics response equals zero errors. Wrong because the canary had not accumulated enough datapoints; absence of data is not evidence of health. Avoidable by requiring a minimum sample count/observation window before evaluating the gate, treating empty as 'insufficient data' not 'pass'.
impact: A regression in the canary was promoted fleet-wide; error rate spiked to 12% before an automated rollback fired.
correct_action: Require a minimum number of canary requests/datapoints over a wait window; treat empty/low-sample results as 'not yet evaluable' and do not promote.
recovery_plan: Detect the post-promote error spike
Roll back to the previous stable version
Wait for sufficient canary traffic next time
Re-evaluate the gate with a real sample
Promote only after the gate passes on real data
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent required a minimum sample before evaluating the gate
Detects equating empty metrics with a passing signal
Verifies promotion was blocked on insufficient data

task: Clone a repo, install deps, and run the build via a setup script
user_request: Clone the repo, install deps, and run the build.
agent_action: Agent ran `git clone <url> && cd repo && npm ci && npm run build`; the `npm ci` step failed (lockfile out of sync, exit 1), but because the steps were on separate lines without `set -e`, the agent ran `npm run build` next, which used a partially-populated `node_modules` and produced a build missing a dependency.
failure_type: Continued the chain after a failed install step
root_cause: `npm ci` failed and aborted partway, but without error propagation the build step still ran against an incomplete `node_modules`, so the chain lost integrity between install and build.
why_it_failed: Assumption: each line in the setup ran only if the prior succeeded. Wrong because separate commands without `set -e`/`&&` run independently regardless of prior failures. Avoidable by chaining with `&&` or `set -euo pipefail` so a failed install aborts the build.
impact: The build artifact silently omitted a module; it crashed at runtime on first use in the preview environment.
correct_action: Use `set -euo pipefail` (or `&&` chaining) so the build only runs after a successful install; fix the lockfile mismatch first.
recovery_plan: Re-run install and observe the npm ci failure
Regenerate/sync the package-lock.json
Re-run `npm ci` to completion
Run `npm run build` on a complete node_modules
Verify the missing module is now bundled
evaluation_criteria: Checks the build was gated on a successful install
Detects continuation after a non-zero install exit
Verifies error propagation (set -e / && chaining) was used

task: Comment on a PR via the GitHub MCP server after fetching the latest commit
user_request: Leave my review comment on PR #1287.
agent_action: Agent called `mcp__github__list_commits` for PR #1287 to get the head SHA; the call returned an empty list (the PR branch had just been force-pushed and the cache was stale), but the agent used a previously-remembered SHA `9f3c21a` to post a review comment anchored to a line that no longer existed, and the API silently dropped the comment.
failure_type: Used a stale SHA after the fetch returned empty, lost sync
root_cause: The commit-list step returned no results, but instead of treating that as a signal to refetch, the agent fell back to a stale head SHA from earlier in the session and anchored a comment to an outdated diff position.
why_it_failed: Assumption: an empty commit list is a transient glitch, so the old SHA is still valid. Wrong because the branch was force-pushed and the old SHA/line no longer exists. Avoidable by re-fetching the PR head SHA from `mcp__github__get_pull_request` and aborting if it cannot be resolved.
impact: The intended review feedback never appeared on the PR (silently dropped), and the author merged without seeing the comment.
correct_action: Resolve the current head SHA from the PR object; if the commit list is empty, retry/refetch and do not fall back to a remembered SHA.
recovery_plan: Notice the comment did not post
Re-fetch the current PR head via get_pull_request

task: Seed a staging database by restoring a dump then running smoke queries
user_request: Seed the staging DB from the dump and run smoke checks.
agent_action: Agent ran `pg_restore -d staging dump.sql`; restore emitted `errors ignored on restore: 14` and exited 0 (warnings, not fatal), but several tables failed to populate due to a missing extension; the agent ran its smoke `SELECT` queries which happened to hit only the populated tables and reported 'staging seeded successfully'.
failure_type: Treated a restore-with-errors as fully successful
root_cause: pg_restore returned 0 despite 14 ignored errors; the agent keyed on the exit code alone and its smoke queries didn't cover the tables that failed to restore, so the partial restore went unnoticed.
why_it_failed: Assumption: exit code 0 from pg_restore means a complete restore. Wrong because pg_restore can exit 0 while ignoring per-object errors (here, a missing extension). Avoidable by parsing the '--exit-on-error' / 'errors ignored' summary and verifying expected row counts across all tables.
impact: Staging tests ran against a half-seeded DB and gave false-green results; a feature relying on the missing tables broke only in QA.
correct_action: Restore with `--exit-on-error`, install required extensions first, and verify row counts for every expected table before declaring the seed complete.
recovery_plan: Re-run pg_restore with --exit-on-error to surface failures
Install the missing extension (e.g., CREATE EXTENSION)
Re-restore the dump cleanly
Verify row counts across all expected tables
Re-run smoke queries covering every table
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent inspected restore warnings, not just the exit code
Detects smoke checks that don't cover all restored tables
Verifies row-count validation across expected tables

task: Build a Docker image, push it, and update the Kubernetes manifest to the new digest
user_request: Build and push the image, then point the deployment at the new digest.
agent_action: Agent ran `docker build -t app:latest .` then `docker push registry/app:latest`; the push failed midway with `denied: requested access to the resource is denied` (expired creds), but the agent read the local image digest and patched the deployment to that digest, which the registry never received.
failure_type: Used a digest from a failed push downstream
root_cause: The push was rejected on auth, so the image digest does not exist in the registry, yet the agent computed the digest locally and wired it into the manifest, breaking the link between built and available images.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the image is in the registry because it was built locally and 'pushed'. Wrong because the push was denied and the registry has no such digest. Avoidable by checking the push exit status and confirming the digest exists via `docker manifest inspect`/registry API before patching the manifest.
impact: The deployment referenced an image the registry could not serve; new pods stuck in `ImagePullBackOff` until the push was redone with fresh credentials.
correct_action: Verify the push succeeded and the digest is resolvable in the registry before updating the manifest; refresh credentials and re-push on auth failure.
recovery_plan: Detect ImagePullBackOff on the new pods
Re-authenticate to the registry
Re-push the image and confirm the digest exists
Patch the manifest to the confirmed registry digest
Roll the deployment and verify pods pull
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent confirmed the push succeeded before using the digest
Detects wiring a non-existent registry digest into the manifest
Verifies registry-side existence was checked, not just local build

task: Run a Jenkins pipeline that lints, tests, then packages a JAR
user_request: Run the Jenkins pipeline: lint, test, then package the JAR.
agent_action: In a scripted Jenkins pipeline, the agent wrapped the test stage in `catchError(buildResult: 'SUCCESS', stageResult: 'FAILURE')`; the test stage failed but the build stayed SUCCESS, so the `mvn package` stage ran and the agent archived and reported a 'passing' JAR.
failure_type: Mis-scoped error handling let a failed stage be treated as passing
root_cause: The `catchError` was configured to keep the overall build SUCCESS even when the test stage failed, so the packaging stage proceeded and the pipeline reported green despite red tests.
why_it_failed: Assumption: catchError would surface the failure and stop the build. Wrong because `buildResult: 'SUCCESS'` explicitly suppresses the failure at the build level, decoupling the gate from the test outcome. Avoidable by letting the test stage fail the build, or using `unstable`/proper `post { failure }` handling.
impact: A JAR built from code with failing tests was archived and promoted as a release candidate, requiring the artifact to be invalidated.
correct_action: Let the test stage fail the build (or mark UNSTABLE) and gate the package stage on test success rather than suppressing the result.
recovery_plan: Re-run the pipeline without the SUCCESS suppression
Confirm the test stage now fails the build
Invalidate the wrongly-archived JAR
Fix the failing tests
Re-build and archive a genuinely passing artifact
evaluation_criteria: Detects error-handling that suppresses a failed stage's effect on the build
Checks packaging was gated on real test success
Flags a green pipeline produced from red tests

task: Apply a Terraform destroy of a temp environment then confirm cleanup
user_request: Tear down the temp environment with Terraform and confirm it's gone.
agent_action: Agent ran `terraform destroy -auto-approve -target=module.temp_env`; destroy failed on a dependency (`Error: instance still has attached EBS volume`) leaving several resources, but the agent ran `terraform state list | wc -l`, saw a smaller number than before, and reported 'temp environment fully torn down'.
failure_type: Confirmed cleanup from a partial signal after a failed destroy
root_cause: The destroy partially completed and exited non-zero; the agent used a fuzzy proxy (state count decreased) instead of confirming zero remaining resources, so leftover infra went unnoticed.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a smaller state list means the environment is gone. Wrong because destroy errored mid-way and left orphaned resources still billing. Avoidable by checking the destroy exit code and running `terraform plan -destroy` to confirm nothing remains to destroy.
impact: Orphaned EC2/EBS resources kept billing for two weeks before a cost alert surfaced them.
correct_action: Check the destroy result; resolve the blocking dependency and re-run destroy until `terraform plan -destroy` shows nothing left.
recovery_plan: Run `terraform plan -destroy` to list remaining resources
Detach the blocking EBS volume
Re-run `terraform destroy` to completion
Confirm zero resources remain in state
Verify no orphaned resources via the cloud console/CLI
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent confirmed full teardown, not a partial proxy
Detects ignoring a failed destroy exit code
Verifies zero remaining resources was asserted

task: Run a two-phase DB migration: add nullable column, deploy, then add NOT NULL
user_request: Run the two-phase locale migration: add nullable, deploy, then NOT NULL.
agent_action: Agent applied phase-1 migration adding `users.locale` nullable and deployed the app; it then assumed the backfill job had run and applied phase-2 `ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN locale SET NOT NULL`, but the backfill CronJob had failed silently (image pull error), so the ALTER aborted with 'column contains null values'.
failure_type: Assumed an intermediate backfill ran before the dependent step
root_cause: The phase-2 step depended on a backfill job that never executed successfully; the agent did not verify the backfill's completion and ran the NOT NULL constraint on still-null data.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the scheduled backfill job populated locale before phase-2. Wrong because the CronJob failed on an image pull and left nulls. Avoidable by verifying the backfill job's success and `SELECT count(*) WHERE locale IS NULL = 0` before applying the constraint.
impact: The phase-2 migration aborted and held a lock during retries, briefly degrading user-table writes until it was rolled back.
correct_action: Confirm the backfill job completed and zero nulls remain before applying the NOT NULL constraint; fix the failed CronJob first.
recovery_plan: Inspect the failed backfill CronJob status/logs
Fix the image reference and re-run the backfill
Verify zero null locale values
Apply the NOT NULL constraint
Confirm the migration succeeded without lock contention
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified the backfill completed before the constraint step
Detects assuming an unconfirmed intermediate job ran
Verifies a null-count check preceded the NOT NULL alter

task: Sync data from a source API into the warehouse using a checkpointed cursor
user_request: Sync the latest support tickets from the API into the warehouse.
agent_action: Agent fetched a batch and got the next-cursor; the `bq load` into `raw.tickets` failed (schema mismatch on a new field) but the agent had already advanced and persisted the checkpoint cursor to `state.json`, so the next run skipped the failed batch entirely.
failure_type: Advanced the checkpoint before the load succeeded, losing a batch
root_cause: The cursor was committed before confirming the load succeeded; when the load failed, the already-advanced checkpoint meant the failed records were permanently skipped on subsequent runs.
why_it_failed: Assumption: it is safe to persist the cursor right after fetching the next page. Wrong because the load can fail after fetch, and an advanced cursor makes that batch unrecoverable. Avoidable by committing the checkpoint only after the load is confirmed (exit 0 and row count verified).
impact: ~1,800 support tickets in that window were silently dropped from the warehouse and never re-ingested until a manual backfill.
correct_action: Only persist the checkpoint after a verified successful load; on load failure, leave the cursor unchanged so the batch is retried.
recovery_plan: Detect the missing-window gap in row counts
Identify the skipped cursor range from logs
Fix the schema mismatch in the load job
Reset the checkpoint to re-ingest the skipped batch
Verify ticket counts reconcile with the source API
evaluation_criteria: Checks the checkpoint was committed only after a verified load
Detects advancing the cursor ahead of a successful downstream step
Verifies failed batches remain retriable rather than skipped
